items.title: Money Stuff: Private Markets Are the New AI Markets
items.summary: Private beta Ten years ago I might have told a story like this. There are a bunch of companies in the world. As the economy grows, their profits will grow. If you buy their stocks, you will get a share of that growth. If you are a normal person saving for retirement, that’s a good thing to do: You want your savings to grow, and owning a share of growing corporate profits in a growing economy is a good way to do that. [1] The easiest way to do that is to just buy all the stocks in proportion to their market capitalizations, for instance in an index fund. Maybe you can do better than that: Maybe you can buy the companies that will grow a lot and avoid the companies that will go bankrupt. But that requires luck and skill and, crucially, it is zero-sum : If you buy the good companies and avoid the bad ones, that means someone else is buying the bad ones and avoiding the good ones, oops for them. Similarly, you could buy lottery tickets or day-trade stock options to get more than your share of economic growth. Same problem, though: Maybe you can get some extra return by winning the lottery, but that’s not a viable plan for everyone . Conventionally, owning a broad slice of the stock market gives you “beta”: It gives you exposure to the market return, which over the long term is mostly positive. Everything else — trying to beat the market by picking the right stocks or options or lottery tickets — gives you “alpha”: It gives you returns to skill, it gives you outperformance (or underperformance), it gives you something other than the broad market return. Beta is generally positive: Everyone can get rich owning the stock market. Alpha is generally zero-sum: Anyone’s outperformance requires someone else’s underperformance. There’s one other thing that doesn’t fit neatly into these categories. Some companies are not public; they don’t trade on the exchange, and their stocks do not contribute to the market return. Some companies are early-stage tech startups in someone’s garage; others were taken private in leveraged buyouts by private equity firms. Institutional investors can invest in those companies through private equity or venture capital funds. Is that alpha or beta? Some of both. It stands to reason that the smartest private investors would cherry-pick the best companies, help run them well, and get higher returns than the broad average of the public markets. But also, you know, these are companies, they participate in economic growth, the goal is for them to one day (re)join the public markets, and they will have some correlation to the public market return. Even in 2016, the lines were blurring a bit. I started writing that “private markets are the new public markets” in 2015 : Startups were staying private longer and raising more money than they...

Money Stuff: Bank of America Missed Some Bad Guys
items.summary: AML It is sort of the job of big US banks to catch terrorists and drug dealers, but not all of them. Be reasonable. If you are a big bank and you have 10 million customers with checking accounts, it stands to reason that, say, 1,000 of them might deal drugs from time to time. If you report 700 of them to the police, that’s quite helpful in fighting crime. If you miss the other 300, fine. Nobody expects you to identify every drug dealer who keeps cash at your bank. But if you only report 200 of the drug dealers, you arguably are not taking your enforcement responsibilities seriously, and you have to pay a big fine . Those numbers are made up, and I don’t know the actual threshold at which a bank will get in trouble. Obviously it is in some sense unknowable; it’s not like the police catch all the drug dealers either, so you never know the denominator. On the other hand, you do apparently have to catch 100% of your customers who are Jeffrey Epstein . You could have an old-timey model in which every customer who wants to open a checking account walks into the bank and sits down with a bank officer who shakes her hand and looks her in the eye and asks her some questions about what line of work she’s in, and if the potential customer is nervous and twitchy and smells like drugs, the bank officer declines her business. But if she’s a smooth and persuasive and presentable drug dealer then the bank officer will give her a checking account and that’s fine, that’s life, nobody’s perfect. This is not a realistic model for large modern banks, though, and these days what happens is that you have millions of accounts and some statistical system for flagging suspicious ones. The system has some list of features that are predictive of drug dealing, and it scores each account based on how many of those features it displays and to what extent. If the statistical system says “hey this account looks a lot like a drug dealer,” it will escalate the account to a human reviewer, who will take a look and either (1) say “nah system, this is just a misunderstanding” or (2) report to the police. If the statistical system says “hey this account has one or two characteristics that look a leeettle like maybe there’s some drug dealing,” though, it will probably keep that to itself. There are so many accounts, and you can’t be troubling the human reviewers with every little suspicion. The statistical system has some method of weighting the features to generate a risk score, and every account will have some score between “0% drug dealer” and “100% definitely drug dealer,” and there will be some threshold — 30% or 70% or whatever, I don’t know — at which accounts are flagged to humans. And if you are in charge of the bank’s drug-dealer-catching function, you have a dial you can turn...

items.title: Money Stuff: They Found Some Walter Victims
items.summary: “No victims” The basic story of Mark Walter and TWG Global, his holding company, is that TWG owns some insurance companies, and those insurance companies would raise money by selling annuities to customers, and Walter would control how that money was invested, and he would lend some of the money to himself to buy sports teams. Insurance regulators have pretty strict rules about related-party transactions, for reasons that are obvious if you think for a minute about the phrase “lend some of the money to himself to buy sports teams.” When an insurance company is lending its boss money to buy sports teams , it is taking different and spicier credit risk than it would be if it were just buying normal bonds of unaffiliated companies. But TWG’s insurance companies would make a lot of those loans through third parties, which would then turn around and lend the money back to TWG’s businesses. And the insurance companies’ financial statements would not count those loans as related-party loans. Eventually federal prosecutors and insurance regulators started asking questions. “After receiving subpoenas, those insurers disclosed more than $20 billion of loans that should have been labeled as affiliated transactions, but weren’t .” Bad. At the same time, though, owning sports teams has been a lucrative business in recent years, and as far as I can tell it has all worked out great? TWG put out a statement in August saying so: Affiliated transactions should be properly disclosed, but to state that they “generally” have the potential to “loot” the insurer is untrue. The reality is that Group 1001 [ the TWG insurance group ] has invested in real assets that are performing well; the insurance companies have recognized significant income from the investments and no policyholders have lost money because of these transactions. The statement also said: “There is no victim here. No one has been harmed, and no one has claimed they were harmed.” I have pondered that claim a few times . It can’t quite be true. If the world had known the true level of the insurance companies’ affiliated transactions, then … something. Something. Like: Insurance regulators would have demanded that the insurance companies have more capital to offset the increased risk of all those affiliate transactions. Ratings agencies would have given the assets lower ratings, and the insurance companies would have responded by having higher capital to preserve their own financial-strength ratings. Ratings agencies would have given the insurance companies lower ratings, and they would have had to pay higher interest rates on the annuities they sold. Financial advisers would have read the disclosures, said “hmm this sounds risky,” and recommended that their customers look elsewhere for annuities, again...

items.title: Money Stuff: Don’t Bet Against the Sports Bets
items.summary: Money Stuff Swaps, chargers, BDCs, Hood, puzzles. Kalshi gaming regulation You know what’s funny? There is a real legal dispute about whether Kalshi and other prediction markets should be allowed to offer sports bets without complying with state gaming laws. Kalshi and the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission take the view that (1) Kalshi is federally regulated by the CFTC, (2) sports bets are “swaps” under federal regulation, (3) federal regulation preempts state gaming regulation, so (4) buzz off, states. Many states disagree, and there has been litigation around the country. (We have talked about this several times .) Two federal appellate courts have sided with the states, but another has sided with Kalshi. The state that lost that last case (New Jersey) is asking the Supreme Court to review it, and last week 39 states filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s request. So did the National Football League . I assume that the Supreme Court will take the case. I have no idea what it will decide. I think this is a tough question, courts have disagreed on the answer, it is all pretty politically charged, the Supreme Court can kind of do whatever it wants, and I have no real model of what it will want. I could not tell you the probability that Kalshi will win and get to continue offering sports bets. So, out of muscle memory, I fire up Kalshi to check that probability. “Supreme Court Will Rule Kalshi Sports Bets Are Legal, Yes/No,” where is it? But Kalshi doesn’t list that contract ! [1] Here’s “ A Kalshi Contract on the Legality of Kalshi Contracts ,” by Joseph Grundfest: This note proposes that Kalshi list a "Kalshi Sports Legality" contract indexed to the outcome of United States Supreme Court litigation addressing whether Kalshi's sports-indexed contracts are federally regulated in a manner that preempts state law. Kalshi has previously listed at least 16 contracts indexed to Supreme Court determinations. No rule or regulation prevents Kalshi from listing the proposed contract. The proposed contract would provide a market estimate of the probability that the Supreme Court rules that Kalshi's sports-indexed contracts are legal. The contract would thereby create valuable hedging opportunities for Kalshi investors. It would also create hedging value for Kalshi customers who might lose access to Kalshi markets. These hedging rationales are more substantial than rationales Kalshi presents to support other Kalshi contracts, such as contracts indexed to parlays or to specific in-game events, such as whether the first play in a football game leads to a touchdown. Money Stuff: Pre-IPO Perpetual Futures Swap ETF
items.summary: Money Stuff MANGOS, prime, longshots, buffet. MANGOS What is the best way to get economic exposure to Anthropic stock right now? There are bad answers ( expensive SPVs , fake SPVs ). Here are two arguably good answers: Just own Anthropic stock. Own perpetual futures on Anthropic stock on Hyperliquid. The first answer is pretty self-explanatory. Anthropic has stock, and people own it, and owning it gives you economic exposure to Anthropic stock. There are problems. Not just anyone can own Anthropic stock. It is a private company, and its shares do not trade on an exchange. You more or less need to get the stock from Anthropic , so this approach requires you to be an employee or a venture capital investor in one of its funding rounds or an effective altruist hedge fund manager . For most of us, that rules out this approach entirely. But there is another problem, even if you can get the stock. The other problem is that Anthropic stock is fairly illiquid. [1] You can’t easily sell it, until it goes public. Owning the stock gives you economic exposure to the stock, but you don’t get to decide how long you keep that exposure. And you don’t really know its price . So you do have economic exposure to the stock — if it goes up, your stock is worth more — but you don’t necessarily know how much. The second answer is weirder. Hyperliquid Labs runs a leading platform for trading perpetual futures contracts. Traditionally perpetual futures are a crypto thing, a way to make levered bets on cryptocurrencies, they have expanded into stocks and commodities. Kalshi launched an S&P 500 futures contract and is working on perpetual futures for individual stocks. Perpetual futures contracts are basically bets on prices: One person goes long, one person goes short, the short pays the long if the stock goes up, and the long pays the short if it goes down. A perpetual futures contract on an individual public stock is just a levered bet on that stock, and by arbitrage it will closely track the price of the underlying stock. If SpaceX stock trades at $167.60, and SpaceX perpetual futures trade at $165, arbitrageurs will buy the futures and sell the stock until the prices are in line, etc. [2] But perpetual futures on private stock have no arbitrage mechanism to make the price correct. If Anthropic perpetual futures trade at $120, while Anthropic’s stock is at $100, arbitrageurs cannot sell the futures and buy the stock until the prices converge: They can sell the futures, but they can’t buy the stock. [3] Also, how do you even know that “Anthropic’s stock is at $100”? Anthropic doesn’t trade liquidly or publicly, so you don’t know its price from minute to minute, the way you know the price of the futures. I came across some beautiful chanterelles at Uwajimaya while filming our Japanese Pantry Guide the other day, and while I normally make this pasta dish with much less expensive mushrooms, I love chanterelles enough that I couldn't resist. The good news is that the specific mushroom really isn't important here. Button or cremini mushrooms work great. So do shiitake, portobello, hen of the woods, oyster mushrooms, or virtually any mixture you can find at the grocery store or farmers market. The important part is giving the mushrooms enough heat and time to actually brown them before you start building the sauce. This is one of those pastas where the sauce doesn't really exist until the very end. You start by browning the mushrooms hard in olive oil (I like to throw in a thyme or rosemary sprig while the mushrooms sauté and fish it out later), then add a little onion or shallot and garlic.
